Title: Sensor-Drift Compensation in Electronic-Nose-Based Gas Recognition Using Knowledge Distillation
Abstract: Environmental changes and sensor aging can cause sensor drift in sensor array responses (i.e., a shift in the measured signal/feature distribution over time), which in turn degrades gas classification performance in real-world deployments of electronic-nose systems. Previous studies using the UCI Gas Sensor Array Drift Dataset as a benchmark reported promising drift compensation results but often lacked robust statistical validation and may overcompensate for drift by suppressing class-discriminative variance. To address these limitations and rigorously evaluate improvements in sensor-drift compensation, we designed two domain adaptation tasks based on the UCI electronic-nose dataset: (1) using the first batch to predict remaining batches, simulating a controlled laboratory setting, and (2) using Batches 1 through n−1 to predict Batch n, simulating continuous training data updates for online training. Then, we systematically tested three methods—our semi-supervised knowledge distillation method (KD) for sensor-drift compensation; a previously benchmarked method, Domain-Regularized Component Analysis (DRCA); and a hybrid method, KD–DRCA—across 30 random test-set partitions on the UCI dataset. We showed that semi-supervised KD consistently outperformed both DRCA and KD–DRCA, achieving up to 18% and 15% relative improvements in accuracy and F1-score, respectively, over the baseline, proving KD’s superior effectiveness in electronic-nose drift compensation. This work provides a rigorous statistical validation of KD for electronic-nose drift compensation under long-term temporal drift, with repeated randomized evaluation and significance testing, and demonstrates consistent improvements over DRCA on the UCI drift benchmark.

Authors: Zhifang Liang, Dongming Chen, Liu Yang, Ping-Fang Xie, Feng-Chun Tian, Bei Liu
Title: An Online Test-Time Adaptive Drift Compensation Network for Electronic Nose
Source: IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement
Abstract: Sensor drift is a common problem in electronic nose (e-nose) systems. In recent years, research on this problem has also made significant progress, and various drift compensation methods have emerged. Although these methods have achieved impressive results in terms of recognition accuracy, they often fail to fully account for the drift situation in online environments. Therefore, an online test-time adaptive drift compensation network (OTTA-DriftNet) is proposed for e-nose in this article, which can adaptively adjust the prediction model online to address drift phenomena. OTTA-DriftNet consists of two steps: generating source model and online test-time adaptation (OTTA). In the generating source model phase, the data are preprocessed, and the source model is trained using the distribution-aligned nondrifted source-domain data. In the OTTA phase, the pretrained source model is first used to initialize the teacher model in the network. Then, based on OTTA, the student model gradually adapts to the changes in drifted data, ultimately achieving efficient online recognition of unlabeled drifted data. In this process, the parameters of the teacher model and the student model (prediction model) learn from each other using the knowledge distillation (KD) mechanism and are continuously optimized and updated. Due to the complexity of e-nose data and its temporal nature, attention mechanisms and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks are used during model construction to enhance the model’s feature processing capability. The experimental results show that the proposed OTTA-DriftNet can effectively address the drift problem in the online situation on a public dataset and outperforms the existing methods in terms of recognition accuracy.

Authors: Zhifang Liang, Dongming Chen, Liu Yang
Title: Online Test-Time Adaptation for Electronic Nose Drift Compensation
Source: 2024 6th International Conference on Electronic Engineering and Informatics (EEI)
Abstract: Sensor drift is a common problem in E-nose systems. In recent years, research on this problem has made significant progress, and various drift compensation methods have emerged. Although these methods have achieved notable performance in recognition accuracy, they seldom deal with the drift problem in the online scenarios. Therefore, this paper proposes an E-nose drift compensation method based on online test-time adaptation. The method first removes abnormal data using data preprocessing methods to ensure the training quality of the model. Then uses a mutually learning teacher-student distillation model with continuous updates to adapt the model to drift data. The online recognition of unlabeled drift data is finally realized. The ability of the test-time adaptation (TTA) to adaptively adjust to the unlabeled drift data also makes the model highly robust and adaptable. Experimental results on public datasets show that the proposed method is effective enough to deal with the drift problem in the online case, and it also exhibits a high recognition rate compared to other state-of-the-art approaches.

Title: Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolutionary Strategy for Drift Correction of Electronic Nose Data

Authors: Ting-Han Shi, Kea-Tiong Tang, Shih-Wen Chiu, Pang-Chun Liu
Title: Meta-Learning on Electronic-Nose Time Series for Long-Term Drift Compensation in Metal Oxide Gas Sensor Arrays
Source: 2026 IEEE International Symposium on Olfaction and Electronic Nose (ISOEN)
Abstract: Long-term drift in metal oxide gas sensor arrays remains a major obstacle for reliable electronic-nose deployment. Recent work has shown that meta-learning can mitigate drift on legacy feature-engineered datasets, but the behavior of modelagnostic meta-learning (MAML) on raw time-series responses from modern electronic noses is still unclear. In this work we present an initial empirical study of MAML on the “Long-term drift behavior in metal oxide gas sensor arrays” one-year dataset, which provides 700 recordings from a 62-sensor commercial electronic nose with both raw signals and pre-extracted features. We first establish a supervised 1D residual network baseline trained on early days and tested on later days, confirming strong accuracy degradation due to drift. We then define day-wise and batched-day meta-learning tasks and apply MAML directly to the raw multi-channel sensor responses under few-shot adaptation. Our results show that naïvely applying MAML on this dataset does not automatically outperform a well-tuned supervised baseline; instead, performance is sensitive to task construction and optimization details. We situate these findings with respect to prior feature-based meta-learning work and discuss implications for future electronic-nose algorithms on long-term drift datasets.
